verses.text: They took their journey from Elim, and all the congregation of the children of Israel came to the wilderness of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departing out of the land of Egypt.
The whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness;

and the children of Israel said to them, “We wish that we had died by Yahweh’s hand in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots, when we ate our fill of bread, for you have brought us out into this wilderness, to kill this whole assembly with hunger.”

Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
It shall come to pass on the sixth day, that they shall prepare that which they bring in, and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.”
Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel, “At evening, then you shall know that Yahweh has brought you out from the land of Egypt;
and in the morning, then you shall see Yahweh’s glory; because he hears your murmurings against Yahweh. Who are we, that you murmur against us?”

Moses said, “Now Yahweh shall give you meat to eat in the evening, and in the morning bread to satisfy you; because Yahweh hears your murmurings which you murmur against him. And who are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against Yahweh.”
Moses said to Aaron, “Tell all the congregation of the children of Israel, ‘Come near before Yahweh, for he has heard your murmurings.’”
As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, Yahweh’s glory appeared in the cloud.
Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,

“I have heard the murmurings of the children of Israel. Speak to them, saying, ‘At evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread: and you shall know that I am Yahweh your God.’”
In the evening, quail came up and covered the camp; and in the morning the dew lay around the camp.
When the dew that lay had gone, behold, on the surface of the wilderness was a small round thing, small as the frost on the ground.
When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, “What is it?” For they didn’t know what it was. Moses said to them, “It is the bread which Yahweh has given you to eat.”

This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded: “Gather of it everyone according to his eating; an omer  a head, according to the number of your persons, you shall take it, every man for those who are in his tent.”
The children of Israel did so, and gathered some more, some less.
When they measured it with an omer, he who gathered much had nothing over, and he who gathered little had no lack. They gathered every man according to his eating.
Moses said to them, “Let no one leave of it until the morning.”
Notwithstanding they didn’t listen to Moses, but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and became foul: and Moses was angry with them.
They gathered it morning by morning, everyone according to his eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.
On the sixth day, they gathered twice as much bread, two omers for each one, and all the rulers of the congregation came and told Moses.

He said to them, “This is that which Yahweh has spoken, ‘Tomorrow is a solemn rest, a holy Sabbath to Yahweh. Bake that which you want to bake, and boil that which you want to boil; and all that remains over lay up for yourselves to be kept until the morning.’”
They laid it up until the morning, as Moses asked, and it didn’t become foul, and there were no worms in it.
Moses said, “Eat that today, for today is a Sabbath to Yahweh. Today you shall not find it in the field.
Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath. In it there shall be none.”
On the seventh day, some of the people went out to gather, and they found none.
Yahweh said to Moses, “How long do you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws?
Behold, because Yahweh has given you the Sabbath, therefore he gives you on the sixth day the bread of two days. Everyone stay in his place. Let no one go out of his place on the seventh day.”
So the people rested on the seventh day.
The house of Israel called its name Manna,  and it was like coriander seed, white; and its taste was like wafers with honey.

Moses said, “This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded, ‘Let an omer-full of it be kept throughout your generations, that they may see the bread with which I fed you in the wilderness, when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.’”
Moses said to Aaron, “Take a pot, and put an omer-full of manna in it, and lay it up before Yahweh, to be kept throughout your generations.”
As Yahweh commanded Moses, so Aaron laid it up before the Testimony, to be kept.
The children of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They ate the manna until they came to the borders of the land of Canaan.
Now an omer is one tenth of an ephah.

footnotes.content: Two months from Egypt, and they're already walking through the wilderness of Sin—a place whose very name sounds forbidding. The Lord brought them here not to lose them, but to teach them something they couldn't learn in the comfort of Elim.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Watch what hunger does: it loosens the tongue and clouds the heart. In just two months, the whole camp is murmuring—not quietly, but against the very leaders God appointed. I've seen this in myself too, how quickly confidence turns to complaint when the stomach complains.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How memory lies to us. They remember the meat pots and bread in Egypt—forget the taskmaster's whip, the murdered sons. Fear rewrites our past to make it prettier. But the Lord hears what's underneath: they don't really want Egypt back; they're terrified He can't feed them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The word is a test. God will send bread from heaven—not as a free gift, but as proof of His law and His character. He's asking them: Will you trust what I say about how to live, or will you lean on your own hungers?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Double bread on the sixth day—the Lord is building the Sabbath into the rhythm before they've even heard it commanded. He writes His rest into the dust itself, into the way the manna falls. That's how deeply He wants them to understand: rest isn't earned, it's given.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses speaks to them with a gentle correction: the deliverance wasn't his doing—it was Yahweh's. They'll know it in the evening when meat comes; they'll see it in the morning when bread falls. Not by words, but by God's own hand opening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: There's something cutting in Moses' question—"Who are we?"—as if to say: You think we brought you here? We're only servants. Your murmuring goes straight past us to the Lord Himself. That's both humbling and true: our complaints, our doubts, they all reach heaven.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses says the same thing twice because it needs to sink in: your anger isn't with us—it's with God. When we shake our fist at those who lead us faithfully, we're really shaking it at the One who sent them. He speaks the truth not harshly, but with the clarity of love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses tells Aaron to call them to come near—not to run or flee. The Lord heard their murmurings and rather than scattering them, He draws them close. There's mercy here: the wilderness will cure them not through punishment, but through presence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They turned to look—and there it was, the glory of Yahweh in the cloud. Not hidden or distant, but visible, unmissable. In a moment, their fear softens. The Lord doesn't leave them guessing about whether He hears their complaints; He shows Himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh speaks to Moses—always through the intermediary, always with order and purpose. The Lord doesn't abandon His word to the chaos of wandering hunger; He speaks clearly what will happen next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: I have heard. Those words carry weight: the murmuring reaches the throne. The Lord promises both evening meat and morning bread, and more than feeding—a revelation: "You shall know that I am Yahweh your God." Hunger will teach them who He is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The quail came up and covered the camp—such abundance that it fell like a blanket. The Lord keeps His word with extravagance, not parsimony. And with the dew in the morning comes manna: a provision so regular and layered that the wilderness becomes home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the wilderness ground, where nothing normally grows, there lies a small round thing—small as frost. The Lord's provision is humble, not flashy. It looks almost insignificant until you gather it and feed your family. That's how grace often arrives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "What is it?" they ask. The word manna means just that—a question. But Moses answers for them: It is the bread Yahweh has given you. Not mystery to stay hidden, but mystery revealed as love in action. What He sends is meant to be understood.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An omer a head—the Lord's measure is personal and fair. Not some each get more than they need while others starve, but each gathers according to the size of their household. From the start, the manna teaches: God's provision is ordered by justice, not caprice.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some gathered much, some less—not from greed or laziness, but maybe age or circumstance. The Lord allows His people to gather at their own pace; He doesn't force uniformity. Yet the miracle will show: it all comes out equal in the end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: This is the miracle hidden in provision: he who gathered much had nothing over, he who gathered little had no lack. The Lord is leveling the ground with something more powerful than law—with a wonder that teaches the heart. Enough is always enough.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Leave none of it until morning—an instruction hidden in a test. The Lord is teaching them trust: don't hoard, don't fear tomorrow will find you empty. I've learned this lesson slowly, and it still challenges my heart on difficult days.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some didn't listen. They kept manna for the morning, and it bred worms and became foul. The Lord allows the consequences to teach what words alone cannot: this provision comes fresh each day, not from your cleverness or forethought. That's a hard lesson for people who've learned to hoard.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Morning by morning—a discipline of grace. The manna requires them to wake and gather every day, to depend not on yesterday's work but on today's provision. It's both a rhythm and a rope: it binds them to the moment and to the Lord's faithfulness in the moment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On the sixth day, twice as much—and the rulers notice it. The Lord's design is so careful that the leaders of the people see it, understand it, report it to Moses. The miracle isn't just happening; it's observable, reasonable, and worth telling about.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses explains: tomorrow is a solemn rest, a holy Sabbath. The double manna makes sense now—the Lord has built the Sabbath into the provision itself. Before they rest, the bread is ready. Before they obey, they see the reason. The Lord teaches by showing, not only by commanding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They laid it up until morning, and it didn't become foul, and there were no worms. The manna kept for the Sabbath doesn't spoil—a small miracle that whispers louder than thunder: obey, and you will see that I keep my word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Eat that today, for today is a Sabbath to Yahweh. You shall not find it in the field. The Lord is generous enough to say it plainly: on this day, rest. Don't work, don't search, don't strain. He has already provided. Be still and know.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Six days you shall gather it, but on the seventh day is the Sabbath—in it there shall be none. The rhythm is clear and unbreakable: six and one, work and rest, gathering and trusting. The Lord structures time itself to turn our hearts toward Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Some of the people went out on the seventh day anyway, and found none. Hard lessons for hard hearts. The Lord doesn't change the rules because someone didn't believe them. Sabbath is Sabbath, and the manna proves it by its absence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: How long do you refuse to keep my commandments and my laws? There's both exasperation and a father's waiting in that question. The Lord isn't asking for an answer; He's asking them to hear how their hearts sound when they refuse Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Because Yahweh has given you the Sabbath—notice the order. The gift comes first, then the obedience. The Lord doesn't ask for what He hasn't already provided the strength to give. Let no one go out of his place on the seventh day: stay, rest, belong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: So the people rested on the seventh day. After all the murmuring and testing, they finally obey. And there, in that simple rest, they touch something they've never touched before: the Lord's own rhythm, the pulse that beats underneath creation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The house of Israel called its name Manna, and it was like coriander seed, white; and its taste was like wafers with honey. So ordinary and so sweet—the Lord's provision carries both the simplicity of seeds and the delight of honey. It's enough and it's good.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Let an omer-full be kept throughout your generations—Moses preserves a memory. The jar of manna becomes a witness, a tangible reminder: I fed you in the wilderness. Every generation that sees it hears the Lord whisper: I have always been faithful.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses tells Aaron to keep it before the Lord—not hidden in a home, but placed where worship happens. The bread from heaven becomes more than food; it becomes a sign of what God is willing to do, placed at the heart of His people's faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As Yahweh commanded Moses, so Aaron laid it up before the Testimony. Obedience flows through the chain: the Lord speaks to Moses, Moses speaks to Aaron, Aaron acts. The orders are kept because the Lord is trustworthy all the way down the line.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The children of Israel ate the manna forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. For four decades, the wilderness floor blooms with bread. It's a mercy so long and so constant that it becomes the fabric of a whole people's life—tested, fed, shaped, and brought home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An omer is one tenth of an ephah—a note for the record, a measure clarified for those who come after. The Lord doesn't leave His people guessing about the size of grace. It can be weighed, counted, and remembered. That's how real His care is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
